'''''Lactuca serriola''''', also called '''prickly lettuce''',<ref name=GRIN>{{GRIN | accessdate = December 17, 2017}}</ref> '''milk thistle'''<ref name=GRIN/> (not to be confused with ''[[Silybum marianum]]'', also called milk thistle), '''compass plant''',<ref name = GRIN /> and '''scarole''',<ref name=GRIN/> is an [[annual plant|annual]] or [[biennial plant]] in the tribe [[Cichorieae]] within the family [[Asteraceae]]. It has a slightly fetid [[odor]] and is commonly considered a [[weed]] of [[orchard]]s, roadsides and field crops.<ref>{{Cite book |last1 =Everitt |first1 =JH | last2 =Lonard | first2 = RL | last3 = Little | first3 = CR |title=Weeds in South Texas and Northern Mexico | publisher=Texas Tech University Press |location=Lubbock |year=2007 | isbn = 978-0-89672-614-7}}</ref>  It is the closest wild relative of cultivated lettuce (''[[Lactuca sativa]]'' L.).

''Lactuca serriola'' is native to Eurasia and North Africa, and has become [[Naturalisation (biology)|naturalized]] elsewhere.

==Description==
[[Image:Lactuca serriola.jpg|thumb|The long auricles at the base of the leaf might appear clasping.]]
[[Image:Kompassla 08-07-2006 9.39.08.JPG|thumb|Close-up of ''Lactuca serriola'' leaf showing fine spines]]

''Lactuca serriola'' has a spineless reddish stem, containing a milky latex, growing up to {{convert|2|m}}.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book|last1=Elias|first1=Thomas S.|title=Edible Wild Plants: A North American Field Guide to Over 200 Natural Foods|last2=Dykeman|first2=Peter A.|publisher=[[Sterling Publishing|Sterling]]|year=2009|isbn=978-1-4027-6715-9|location=New York|pages=104|oclc=244766414|orig-year=1982}}</ref>

The [[leaves]] get progressively smaller as they reach its top. They are [[Leaf shape|oblong or lanceolate, often pinnately lobed]] and (especially for the lower leaves), waxy grey green. Fine spines are present along the veins and leaf edges. The undersides have whitish veins. They emit [[latex]] when cut.

The flower heads are {{convert|1-1.5|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} wide,<ref name=":2" /> pale yellow, often tinged purple, with 12–20 [[ray flowers]] but no [[disc flowers]]. The bracts are also often tinged purple. It flowers from July until September in the northern hemisphere. The [[achenes]] are grey, tipped with bristles. The [[Pappus (flower structure)|pappus]] is white with equal length hairs.<ref name=z/><ref name="The Wild Flower Key">{{cite book|last=Rose |first=Francis|author-link=Francis Rose  |title=The Wild Flower Key |year=1981 |publisher=Frederick Warne & Co|isbn=0-7232-2419-6 |pages=390–391}}</ref>

''Lactuca serriola'' is known as the compass plant because in the sun the upper leaves twist round to hold their margins upright, pointing roughly south or north from the stem.<ref name= "Wild Flowers of Britain and Ireland">{{cite book |last1 =Blamey |first1 =Marjorie | last2 = Fitter| first2 = Richard | last3 = Fitter| first3 = Alistair |title=Wild Flowers of Britain and Ireland|year=2003 |publisher=A&C Black | place = London|isbn=0-7136-5944-0 |pages=294–5}}</ref>

Similar to ''[[Mycelis muralis]]'' but showing more than 5 florets.

==Distribution==
[[File:Lactuca serriola clump.jpg|thumb|upright=1.2|A cluster of nine ''L. serriola'', growing to a height of {{convert|5.5|ft|m|abbr=on}}]]

''Lactuca serriola'' is native to [[Europe]], [[Asia]], and [[North Africa]], and has become [[Naturalisation (biology)|naturalized]] elsewhere.<ref name=GRIN/><ref name=z>{{eFloras|1 |tribe=Cichorieae |first=John L. |last=Strother}}</ref><ref>{{eFloras|2 |family=Asteraceae |first1=Zhu |last1=Shi |first2=Norbert |last2=Kilian}}</ref><ref>[http://luirig.altervista.org/flora/taxa/index1.php?scientific-name=lactuca+serriola Flora Italiana, ''Lactuca serriola'' L.] includes photos, drawings, European distribution map</ref><ref>Cabrera, A. L. 1978. Compositae. 10: 1–726. In A. L. Cabrera (ed.) Flora de la provincia de Jujuy. Instituto Nacional de Tecnología Agropecuaria, Buenos Aires</ref><ref>[http://bie.ala.org.au/species/urn:lsid:biodiversity.org.au:apni.taxon:618061 Atlas of Living Australia]</ref>

==Pathogen resistance==
''Lactuca serriola'' is the wild progenitor of cultivated lettuce (''[[Lactuca sativa]]'') and can be affected by lettuce downy mildew, one of the most serious diseases of lettuce.<ref name=":0" /> ''L. serriola'' has shown resistance to the plant pathogen ''[[Bremia lactucae]]'', the cause of the disease.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|title = New wild Lactuca genetic resources with resistance against Bremia lactucae.|author = Beharav, A.|author2 = Lewinsohn, D.|author3 = Lebeda A.|author4 = Nevo, E.|date = 2006|journal = Genetic Resources and Crop Evolution |volume=53 |issue = 3|pages=467–474|doi = 10.1007/s10722-004-1932-7|s2cid = 279531}}</ref> This pathogen is able to undergo sexual reproduction, and once virulent strains have been produced, can undergo rapid asexual reproductive cycles.<ref name="SPRINGER" /> As a result, there are many strains, which vary in virulence.<ref name =SPRINGER>{{cite journal|last1=Maisonnueve|first1=B|last2=Bellec|first2=Y|last3=Anderson|first3=P|last4=Michelmore|first4=R.W.|title=Rapid mapping of two genes for resistance to downy mildew from ''Lactuca serriola'' to existing clusters of resistance genes |journal=Theoretical and Applied Genetics|date=September 1994|volume=89|issue=1|pages=96–104|doi=10.1007/BF00226989|pmid=24177776|s2cid=12834976}}</ref>

Resistance to ''Bremia lactucae'' in ''Lactuca serriola'' is due to ''Dm'' genes, or single dominant genes.<ref name="SPRINGER" /> Nine of the dominant genes that confer resistance are ''Dml, Dm, Dm3, Dm6, Dml4, Dml5, DmlO,'' ''Dm5/8, Dm10'', ''Dm4, Dm7, Dm11,'' and ''Dm13''.<ref name=":0" /> These genes are mapped in four linkage groups, so the genes within each group will be more likely to be inherited together.<ref name=":0" /> ''Lactuca serriola'' and ''B. lactucae'' have a [[gene-for-gene relationship]],<ref>{{Cite journal|title = Genetic analysis of factors for resistance to downy mildew Bremia lactucae in species of lettuce Lactuca sativa and L. serriola.|author = Farrara, B. F.|author2 = Ilot, T. W.|author3 = Michelmore, R. W.|date = 1987|journal = Plant Pathology |volume=36 | issue=4 |pages=499–514 |doi = 10.1111/j.1365-3059.1987.tb02267.x}}</ref> meaning that each resistance gene in the plant is associated with a specific gene in the pathogen, with avirulence being dominant to virulence.<ref name=":0" /> The possible combinations of these ''Dm'' genes can provide the plant with resistance to multiple strains of ''Bremia lactucae''.<ref name=":0" />

Testing for the presence of new resistance factors is conducted by screening samples of ''L. serriola'' with various isolates of ''B. lactucae.''<ref name=":0" /> Samples of ''L. serriola'' can be found around the world with genetic diversity between populations regarding the ''Dm'' genes.<ref name=":1" /> This genetic diversity is considered a resource for lettuce breeding because it provides a greater variety of genes to be used in response to new strains of ''B. lactucae'', which continually emerge.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /> There is especially high diversity within the Mediterranean area and Southwest Asia, but ''L. serriola'' has established populations on all continents and has the most widespread distribution compared to other ''Lactuca'' species.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|title = Molecular diversity at the major cluster of disease resistance genes in cultivated and wild Lactuca spp|author = Sicard, D.|author2 = Woo, S. S.|author3 = Arroyo-Garcia, R.|author4 = Ochoa, O.|author5 = Nguyen, D.|author6 = Korol, A.|author7 = Nevo, E.|author8 = Michelmore, R.|date = 1999|journal = Theoretical and Applied Genetics |volume=99 |issue = 3–4|pages=405–418 |doi = 10.1007/s001220051251|pmid = 22665172|s2cid = 20828855}}</ref>

==Toxicity==
It can cause [[pulmonary emphysema]] in cattle feeding exclusively on the plant.<ref>{{cite book |title=Common Weeds of the United States |date=1971 |publisher=Dover |location=New York |isbn=0-486-20504-5 |page=[https://archive.org/details/commonweedsofuni00unit/page/426 426] |url=https://archive.org/details/commonweedsofuni00unit/page/426 }}</ref>

==Uses==
''Lactuca serriola'' can be eaten as a [[salad]], although it has something of a bitter taste. Young leaves can be eaten raw or cooked.<ref>{{cite web |title= Lactuca serriola|url=http://www.survival.org.au/bf_lactuca_serriola.php|work=Survival and Self Sufficiency| place = [[Australia|AU]] | accessdate=9 September 2011}}</ref> Older leaves can be steamed.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Nyerges |first1=Christopher |title=Foraging Wild Edible Plants of North America: More than 150 Delicious Recipes Using Nature's Edibles |date=2016 |publisher=Rowman & Littlefield |isbn=978-1-4930-1499-6 |page=188 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RwDHCgAAQBAJ}}</ref> While unsubstantial, its roots have been used as a [[coffee substitute]].<ref>{{Cite book|last=Nyerges|first=Christopher|title=Foraging Washington: Finding, Identifying, and Preparing Edible Wild Foods|publisher=Falcon Guides|year=2017|isbn=978-1-4930-2534-3|location=Guilford, CT|oclc=965922681}}</ref>

Its presence in some ancient deposits has been linked more to its [[soporific]] properties which might suggest ritual use. The [[ancient Greece|Ancient Greeks]] also believed its pungent juice to be a remedy against [[Corneal ulcer|eye ulcers]] and [[Pythagoreans]] called the lettuce ''eunuch'' because it caused urination and relaxed sexual desire.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Detienne|first=Marcel|title=The Gardens of Adonis: Spices in Greek Mythology|publisher=The Humanities Press|year=1977|location=New Jersey|pages=125|translator-last=Lloyd|translator-first=Janet}}</ref> Following its accidental introduction to North America, the [[Navajo people|Navajo]] began to use the plant as a ceremonial [[Vomiting|emetic]].<ref>{{Citation | contribution = Lactuca serriola | url = http://herb.umd.umich.edu/herb/search.pl?searchstring=Lactuca+serriola | title = Ethnobotany | publisher = U Mich}}.</ref> In the island of [[Crete]] in [[Greece]] the leaves and the tender shoots of a variety called maroula (μαρούλα) or agriomaroulo (αγριομάρουλο) are eaten boiled.<ref>{{cite book | first = Kleonikos G [Κλεόνικος Γ. Σταυριδάκης] | last = Stavridakis |script-title= el:Η Άγρια βρώσιμη χλωρίδα της Κρήτης |trans-title=Wild edible plants of Crete |publisher= Rethymnon | place = Crete |year=2006 |isbn = 960-631-179-1}}</ref> It is used by a growing number of [[Jews]] and [[Samaritans]] as the [[Maror]] (bitter herb) on Passover (or [[Pesach]] in Hebrew).{{citation needed|date=April 2019}}

''Lactuca serriola'' contains [[lactucarium]], which is the milky sap (white latex) that flows through the stem of the plant. It is used as a medicinal herb when air-dried. Although the standard definition of lactucarium requires its production from ''[[Lactuca virosa]]'', it was recognized that smaller quantities of lactucarium could be produced in a similar way from ''[[Lactuca sativa]]'' and ''[[Lactuca canadensis]]'' var. ''elongata'', and even that lettuce-opium obtained from ''Lactuca serriola'' or ''[[Lactuca quercina]]'' was of superior quality.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.henriettes-herb.com/eclectic/kings/lactuca_lact_tinc.html|title=King's American Dispensary:Tinctura Lactucarii (U. ==In culture==

The Egyptian god [[Min (god)|Min]] is associated with this species of lettuce. Also, archaeobotanical evidence in Greek archaeological contexts is scanty, although uncarbonised seeds have been retrieved from a 7th-century BC deposit in a sanctuary of [[Hera]] on [[Samos Island|Samos]]. It is also described by [[Theophrastus]]. In mythology, [[Aphrodite]] is said to have laid [[Adonis]] in a lettuce bed, leading to the vegetable's association with food for the dead.<ref>{{Citation | last = Fragiska | first = M | year = 2005 | title = Wild and Cultivated Vegetables, Herbs and Spices in Greek Antiquity | journal = Environmental Archaeology | volume = 10 | number = 1 | pages = 73–82 | doi=10.1179/146141005790083858}}.</ref>
